chunks.body:
A clear result means the satellite record holds no water body, no buffer breach
and no drainage line within the measurement uncertainty of this plot. It is a
statement about the record.

Below the detection floor the record is silent rather than negative. Small
tanks, filled decades before the archive begins, and drains too narrow for the
terrain model all fall into that silence. A clear screening result is a reason
not to prioritise a plot for investigation. It is not an assurance to the
applicant, and it should not be quoted back to one as though it were.
chunks.source: index.html, the no-objection branch of decide()
chunks.title: Finding nothing is not the same as there being nothing

chunks.body:
Four terms make up the budget. The position of a shoreline within a source pixel
contributes about 15 m. The quantisation of the distance transform contributes
about 7 m. One pixel of georeferencing slack contributes about 6 m. The
thumbnail resample and the byte decode contribute nothing, being nearest
neighbour and exact.

Combined in quadrature that is about 20 m, and it attaches to every distance
this tool reports. A distance should never be stated as exact, and two distances
differing by less than the budget should never be described as different.
chunks.source: index.html, ERROR_BUDGET
chunks.title: Every distance in this tool carries about twenty metres of uncertainty

chunks.body:
The budget is dominated by where a shoreline sits inside a source pixel. Every
term this tool adds by its own processing is smaller, and several are zero by
construction.

The practical consequence is that finer encoding, a finer distance transform or
a larger export would buy nothing. The number would gain digits and not
accuracy. Improving on this would take a better source: a surveyed lake boundary
or a fine-resolution elevation model, neither of which is what this tool is
built on.
chunks.source: index.html, the note under the error budget
chunks.title: The error is inherited from the source, not created here

chunks.body:
The narrower of the two buffer regimes sits barely outside the measurement
uncertainty. Under it, most plots near a lake edge come back as refer-to-survey
rather than reject, because the measurement genuinely cannot separate inside
from outside.

The wider regime is comfortably testable and returns decisive results on the
same measurements. This is a fact about the relationship between the rule and
the available data, not a defect in either. It is also the reason a referral
under the narrow regime should be read as unresolved rather than as a near miss.
chunks.source: README, a consequence worth knowing before anyone asks
chunks.title: The narrower buffer is barely testable at this uncertainty

chunks.body:
Distances are the nearest approach over the assumed footprint, so a larger
assumed plot reaches closer to everything and can turn a clear result into a
referral, or a referral into a rejection.

The frontage is operator input, not a measurement of the actual plot. Where it
has been set well above a typical residential footprint, the result describes a
large site and should be read that way. The value used is printed on the
certificate next to the distances it produced, precisely so that a reader can
tell whether it was the right one.
chunks.source: index.html, the plot frontage control and readSite()
chunks.title: The assumed plot size changes the result, and is an input

chunks.body:
The catchment-wide figures — water lost, water surviving, built area on former
water, structures intersecting it — are computed by the extraction step and
loaded from the statistics file for the active city.

They are deliberately not written into this corpus. A total that is copied into
prose goes stale the first time the extraction is re-run over a different date
range, and then two numbers exist for one quantity with nothing to say which is
current. Any catchment total quoted in an answer must come from the loaded
statistics, not from here.
chunks.source: data/<city>/stats.json, printed by the Earth Engine extraction
chunks.title: The catchment totals are read at runtime, not stated here

chunks.body:
Runoff arithmetic here uses a design depth of 60 mm falling in 60 minutes, and
an annual total of 970 mm for the yearly figure.

This value is a placeholder and carries the widest uncertainty of anything in
the tool, roughly plus or minus 24 mm, dominated by the choice of return period
rather than by any measurement. It must be replaced with the published
intensity-duration-frequency figure for this city before any output is relied
on. Every volume the tool reports scales linearly with it, so replacing it
rescales every runoff number at once and changes nothing else.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending IMD Bengaluru intensity-duration-frequency curve or the BBMP stormwater design storm
chunks.title: The design storm used for runoff arithmetic

chunks.body:
Displaced volume is the plot area in square metres, times the design storm depth
in metres, times the change in runoff coefficient. Each of the three inputs is
declared with its own source and its own uncertainty, and the result is reported
to two significant figures with a plausible range rather than as a point value.

The uncertainty is dominated by the design storm and the coefficient change, not
by the plot area. Combined it is large enough that a reader should treat the
figure as an order of magnitude with a direction, and small enough that the
direction is unambiguous: development on open ground sends more water downhill.
chunks.source: index.html, the derived quantities in siteContext()
chunks.title: How the displaced volume is computed

chunks.body:
The volume a plot displaces is a quantity of water. How deep that water stands
somewhere downhill depends on where it goes, what carries it, what is already in
the channel and how fast it drains, none of which this tool holds.

So the volume can be stated and the depth cannot. The volume is still the useful
number, because it is additive: it is what the plot contributes to a total that
a drainage authority holding the network model can convert into a level. This
tool supplies the term. It does not solve the equation.
chunks.source: index.html, the scope of the runoff arithmetic
chunks.title: A displaced volume is not a flood depth

chunks.body:
Water that a tank used to hold, or that a flow path used to carry, does not stop
falling when the tank is filled or the path is built over. It finds another
route, and that route runs across land belonging to someone else.

This is the asymmetry the tool is built to make visible. The benefit of building
on low ground accrues to the plot. The cost accrues downstream, to people with
no part in the application and usually no notice of it. Ranking by how much
catchment a structure blocks is a way of ordering enforcement by that cost
rather than by complaint volume.
chunks.source: README, the three modes
chunks.title: The cost of a blocked flow path is paid downstream

chunks.body:
Flood-prone here means ground standing below the low-ground threshold above the
channel it drains into. It is a topographic statement and nothing more: this
ground is near the level of the water that passes it.

It is not a flood zone, not a return-period map and not a statement that water
has reached this point or will. Ground this low fills first when a channel
exceeds its section and empties last, which is enough to justify a plinth and
retention condition, and not enough to justify a depth, a frequency or a
probability.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, the floodProne definition
chunks.title: What this tool calls flood-prone

chunks.body:
A flow path here is ground that is both low relative to the nearest channel and
carrying the drainage of more than 2 square kilometres of upstream land. Both
conditions have to hold: low ground away from any catchment is a hollow, and a
large catchment on high ground is a ridge above a valley.

Where both hold, water concentrates and runs. Building across such ground does
not merely add runoff, it obstructs runoff that was already passing through, and
the second effect is typically much the larger of the two.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, the flowPath definition
chunks.title: What this tool calls a flow path

chunks.body:
Height above the nearest drainage line is banded rather than read as a depth. At
0 m the plot is at channel level. Up to 1 m it sits inside a water path, which
is the band that triggers a retention and plinth condition. Up to 2 m it is low
ground and counts as flood-prone. Up to 5 m it is marginal. Above that it is
elevated relative to its own drainage.

The bands are ordinal. A plot in a lower band is exposed sooner and longer than
one in a higher band. Nothing in the banding says how much water, or how often.
chunks.source: index.html, the exposure classes in siteContext()
chunks.title: Height above drainage, as an ordinal exposure class

chunks.body:
Sealing a surface has two effects and the volume is the smaller one. Water that
soaks in leaves slowly over hours; water that runs off paving arrives in
minutes. The same rainfall therefore reaches the channel as a taller, narrower
pulse.

A drain sized for the old pulse can be overwhelmed by the new one carrying a
similar total. This is why incremental development floods a catchment that no
single development would have flooded, and why the displaced volume from one
plot understates what that plot contributes to the problem.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending CPHEEO Manual, storm water drainage chapter, on urbanisation effects
chunks.title: Sealing ground changes when the water arrives, not only how much

chunks.body:
The usual drainage calculation estimates a peak rate of flow, which requires a
time of concentration and is used to size a pipe. This tool does not size pipes
and does not have a defensible time of concentration for a single plot.

It uses the volumetric form instead: the depth of the design storm, multiplied
by the plot area, multiplied by the change in runoff coefficient. That yields
the extra volume of water the development sends downhill during one such storm.
It is arithmetic on three stated numbers and can be checked by hand, which is
the reason for preferring it.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending CPHEEO Manual, storm water drainage chapter
chunks.title: Volume displaced, not peak flow

chunks.body:
Holding the displaced volume on site is what sending nothing extra downhill
means. The requirement is not a new obligation: it is the volume this tool has
already computed for the design storm, read as something to retain rather than
as something to shed.

That keeps it checkable on paper. Plot area, storm depth and the change in
runoff coefficient give the volume, and the volume is the requirement. How much
of it the harvesting rule in force already covers is a comparison the officer
makes, with the figure that binds here.
chunks.source: index.html, the retention arithmetic in siteContext
chunks.title: The requirement is the displaced volume, read as something to hold

chunks.body:
Bengaluru already requires rainwater harvesting storage on new plots above a
size threshold. Where that storage is actually built and kept clear, part of the
volume a development displaces is held on site rather than sent downhill.

This matters for how a conditions result should be read. The mitigation being
asked for is usually not a new obligation but the existing one, sized against
the displacement this tool has computed and actually enforced. Comparing the
displaced volume against the required storage is the most useful single
comparison an officer can make with these numbers.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending the BWSSB rainwater harvesting storage requirement for Bengaluru
chunks.title: Some of the displaced volume is already required to be stored on site

chunks.body:
A runoff coefficient is the fraction of rain falling on a surface that leaves it
as surface flow rather than soaking in or evaporating.

Open, unbuilt urban land is taken at 0.3, the middle of the usual pervious band.
A developed plot of roof and paving is taken at 0.85, the middle of the built-up
band. The change is therefore 0.55, with an uncertainty of about 0.15 covering
how much of the plot is actually sealed and what the soil beneath was like.

Both figures are stated defaults pending the published tables, and both are
operator-editable.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending CPHEEO Manual on Sewerage and Sewage Treatment, storm water drainage chapter, or IRC SP:50
chunks.title: Runoff coefficients before and after development

chunks.body:
A volume in cubic metres means little to most readers of a screening note, so
the displaced volume is also expressed as a count of standard 6000 litre water
tankers.

The conversion carries no additional uncertainty of its own and adds no
information. It exists because a number that cannot be pictured is a number that
gets skipped, and the whole purpose of reporting displacement is that someone
weighs it. Where the count is small the honest reading is that a single plot is
a small term in a large sum, which is also worth saying plainly.
chunks.source: Standard water tanker capacity in common use in Bengaluru
chunks.title: Volumes are also given in tankers, to be legible

chunks.body:
A plot's own contribution is its area times the rain that falls on it. What
passes through it is its upstream catchment times the same rain, and on a
channel that can be thousands of times larger.

So for a plot astride a flow path the displaced volume is the wrong headline
number. The relevant quantity is what the obstruction does to water that was
already arriving from uphill, and that depends on the geometry of what is built
and what is left open. This tool reports the catchment size so the scale of that
question is visible; it does not answer it.
chunks.source: index.html, the upstream drainage area fact in siteContext()
chunks.title: What a plot blocks can be far larger than what it sheds

chunks.body:
The land cover classification is conservative about calling a pixel built when
tree canopy covers part of it. Across a green, low-rise catchment that biases
the built-on-former-water area downward.

The hectare figure for construction on former water is therefore a floor rather
than an estimate. The count of individual building footprints intersecting
former water is the stronger number, because it rests on footprint geometry
rather than on a per-pixel land cover call, and it should be preferred whenever
both are available.
chunks.source: README, Known limits
chunks.title: Built-up area under tree canopy is undercounted

chunks.body:
At the source resolution a water body under roughly 0.5 ha is not reliably
detected. The small neighbourhood tanks that a dense settlement swallows first
are exactly the ones below that floor.

So a clear screening result means no recorded water body was found near the
plot. It does not mean there was never a tank there. Where local knowledge, a
place name or a revenue entry says otherwise, the local knowledge is the better
evidence and this tool has nothing to contribute against it.
chunks.source: README, Known limits
chunks.title: Small tanks do not appear in this record at all

chunks.body:
The terrain model resolves catchment-scale drainage. It does not resolve which
order a drain is, how wide it is, or exactly where its alignment runs, and the
buffer that applies depends on all three.

A drainage finding from this tool is therefore always a referral and never a
rejection. It says a channel appears to pass close to this plot and the
alignment record should be checked. If the record shows no drain there, the
record governs and the finding was a false lead, which is an acceptable cost for
a screening step.
chunks.source: README, Known limits
chunks.title: Drain order and drain position are not resolved

chunks.body:
Whether a given storm overwhelms the drains depends on the geometry, gradient,
condition and current blockage of the network carrying the water away. None of
that is in this tool, and none of it is derivable from the satellite record.

So the tool can say how much additional runoff a plot generates and where the
land slopes, and cannot say whether that additional runoff exceeds what the
channel downhill can take. Those are different questions and only the first one
is answerable here.
chunks.source: index.html, the scope of the downstream mode
chunks.title: Nothing here models what the drains can carry

chunks.body:
No surveyed encroachment dataset exists for this catchment. Without one there is
nothing to score against, and any accuracy percentage quoted for this tool would
be invented.

What can be and has been measured is agreement: whether an independent spectral
method reproduces the reference this pipeline depends on, on held-out ground.
That is a weaker claim than accuracy and it is the strongest claim the available
data supports. Asked how accurate this is, the honest answer names that
distinction rather than filling the gap with a number.
chunks.source: README, Accuracy
chunks.title: There is no accuracy figure because there is no ground truth

chunks.body:
The terrain model resolves catchment drainage at a scale far coarser than a
single storm drain, so a route crossing a built-up block says water runs
downhill across it, not that a channel exists there.

What the trace is good for is naming the ground that receives what a plot sheds,
and ranking it by how much catchment concentrates there. What it cannot say is
that the water arrives, because arrival depends on a drain network this tool
does not hold. A downstream finding is a lead for verification, the same way a
drainage finding is.
chunks.source: index.html, traceDownstream and the downstream panel
chunks.title: The traced route follows terrain, not pipes

chunks.body:
Distances are packed into a single byte, so the largest value they can carry is
255. A pixel reading 255 is not 255 m from the feature; it is somewhere beyond
the range the search covered.

The tool prints such a reading as beyond the ceiling rather than as a number,
and any answer that quotes it as a distance is wrong. In practice this only
happens well away from water and drainage, where the exact distance carries no
decision weight anyway — which is why the ceiling was set where it was.
chunks.source: index.html, the metres() formatter
chunks.title: 255 is a ceiling, not a measurement

chunks.body:
Footprints come from Google Open Buildings, kept only where the model's
confidence is at least 0.70 and the footprint is at least 40 square metres. The
filter removes the two failure modes that would otherwise dominate a ranked
list: low-confidence artefacts on bare ground, and sheds.

Each surviving footprint is scored by how much of it sits on former water, how
much sits in a flow path, how much catchment drains through it and how low it
stands. The score orders a queue for verification. It is not a probability that
the structure is unlawful.
chunks.source: Google Open Buildings v3 polygons
chunks.title: Building footprints are filtered before they are ranked

chunks.body:
One export carries measurement rather than colour and is never drawn. Its red
channel is metres to the water edge in the recent record, its green channel is
metres to the water edge in the earliest record, and its blue channel is metres
to the nearest terrain-derived drainage line.

Reading it is a straight byte lookup: no scaling, no interpolation, no rounding
step that could drift. That is why the exported ranges were chosen to fit a byte
in the first place. The plot check samples this file in an offscreen canvas,
with smoothing disabled, at full resolution.
chunks.source: README, Layer channels
chunks.title: buffers.png carries three distances, one per channel

chunks.body:
The second measurement export packs the last year water was recorded at that
pixel, offset from 1983 so it fits a byte and zero means never; the JRC
occurrence percentage, which is the share of all observations in which the pixel
was water; and the height of the ground above the nearest drainage line, in
metres.

Occurrence is the field that separates a tank from a wet season. A pixel that
was water in most observations was a water body. A pixel that was water in a
small minority of them may have been a flooded field, and at this resolution the
two cannot be told apart.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, the history export
chunks.title: history.png carries when water was last seen, how often, and height above drainage

chunks.body:
Upstream drainage area spans several orders of magnitude across one catchment,
so packing it linearly into a byte would spend almost the whole range on the
trunk channel and leave the tributaries indistinguishable. It is packed
logarithmically instead, with a ceiling of 1000 square kilometres, which holds
the relative resolution roughly constant across the range.

This is the one place the tool scales a byte on decode rather than reading it
straight, so the log law is printed on the certificate. The same file also
carries metres to the nearest trunk channel, defined as one draining more than
10 square kilometres, and metres above the lowest point in the study area.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, the hydro export
chunks.title: hydro.png packs upstream area on a log scale

chunks.body:
The routing layer carries one measurement and two reserved channels. Red holds
the flow direction, remapped off the terrain model's native powers of two into a
compact index: eight compass directions, then one code for an outlet and one for
a closed depression, with zero reserved for nodata.

The remap runs before reprojection, so no resampling step ever sees a power of
two and every legal value sits in a contiguous run. That is what lets the
encoding check assert legality directly, because an averaged direction lands
between the codes rather than on one.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, section 14
chunks.title: How the flow-direction layer is packed

chunks.body:
Every distance in this tool is a fast Euclidean distance transform run in UTM,
at 10 m, over a search radius of 48 pixels, which is 480 m of ground. The
transform must run in a metric projection because it returns squared distance in
squared pixels and only becomes metres when a pixel has a length.

The 10 m step is chosen to stay coarser than the exported pixel. If the
transform were finer than the raster it is packed into, the export would average
adjacent byte codes and produce distances that were never computed. Making it
finer would not make it more accurate.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, distanceMetres()
chunks.title: Distances are a Euclidean transform computed at 10 m in a metric projection

chunks.body:
There is no affine transform stored anywhere. Each exported layer is 2048 by
1195 pixels stretched linearly across the study rectangle, which works out at
about 6.36 m of ground per pixel, and a lookup is arithmetic on the corner
coordinates.

The consequence is that every layer must share those dimensions exactly. If one
did not, its lookups would land on the wrong ground and the tool would return
confident measurements of the wrong place with nothing visibly amiss. An
encoding check gates on matching dimensions before it tests anything else.
chunks.source: index.html, the sampler, and the AOI bounds comment
chunks.title: Every layer is a linear stretch over one rectangle

chunks.body:
Height above nearest drainage and upstream drainage area are both taken
precomputed from MERIT Hydro at 90 m. There is no flow accumulation calculated
here and no digital elevation model processed here.

Height above nearest drainage is the vertical drop from a point to the channel
it drains into. It is an exposure ordinal, not a flood depth: low ground near a
channel floods first and drains last, which is a different statement from
saying how deep the water gets. At 90 m the model resolves catchment drainage
and not the individual drain outside a particular plot.
chunks.source: MERIT Hydro v1.0.1, upstream drainage area and height above nearest drainage
chunks.title: Terrain comes from MERIT Hydro, precomputed, at 90 m

chunks.body:
A lake under a mat of water hyacinth reflects like vegetation, and every water
index reads it as land. Left alone, the pipeline would report the largest lakes
in this catchment as destroyed, which would be both wrong and the most visible
thing on the map.

Land cover classified as water or as flooded vegetation in the recent record is
therefore treated as surviving water and excluded from the loss finding. The
guard is deliberately generous: it trades some real loss going unreported
against the alternative of headline false positives on the two lakes everyone
checks first.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, the still-wet guard
chunks.title: Hyacinth-covered water is protected from being read as destroyed

chunks.body:
A single pixel that changes class between two epochs is usually noise: a shadow,
a misregistration, a wet patch after rain. The loss layer keeps only patches of
at least 4 connected pixels.

This costs the tool genuinely small losses, and that cost is one-directional and
known. It buys a map where every visible patch is large enough to go and look
at, which is what the output is for. A speckled map that is technically more
complete would be less usable and no more true.
chunks.source: gee_blue_grid.js, the connected-pixel filter on lost water
chunks.title: Isolated pixels are dropped before anything is called lost water

chunks.body:
Nothing in this pipeline is trained. Every flag traces to a published dataset
and a stated threshold, which means the reason for any individual flag can be
handed over in full rather than reported as a confidence score.

That is a deliberate trade. A learned model would very likely detect more, and
would be unable to say why it detected any particular thing. For an output whose
purpose is to survive being questioned by the person it is used against, the
reason is worth more than the recall.

The language model reading this explains those reasons. It does not produce them.
chunks.source: README, Accuracy
chunks.title: There is no learned model in the pipeline

chunks.body:
A click is not a point measurement. The tool reads every pixel within a disc the
size of the assumed plot and reduces them.

Distances take the minimum, because a buffer is breached by the nearest corner.
The last year water was recorded and the occurrence take the maximum, because
the strongest evidence of water anywhere under the footprint is the evidence
that matters. Height above drainage takes the minimum, because the lowest ground
under the footprint is what floods.

Each reduction is chosen to be the conservative one for the decision it feeds.
Together they make the screening err toward referral.
chunks.source: index.html, readSite() and sampleCh()
chunks.title: Each reading is reduced over a disc, not taken at a point

chunks.body:
The trace follows the terrain model's own flow-direction field one cell at a
time, stepping 90 m because that is the cell size. Stepping one export pixel
instead would read the same cell over and over and invent precision the source
does not have.

It stops at an outlet, a closed depression, a trunk channel, the edge of the
study area, a cell already visited, or 200 steps. Diagonal steps cross more
ground than orthogonal ones and are counted that way. Structures are counted
where they fall within 150 m of the line.
chunks.source: index.html, traceDownstream
chunks.title: How the downstream route is traced

chunks.body:
Upstream drainage area at a point is the total area of land uphill of it whose
runoff passes through that point on its way downhill. It is measured in square
kilometres and it grows monotonically downstream.

It is the number that separates a plot on a minor slope from a plot astride a
channel that the surrounding neighbourhoods drain through. Blocking the first
displaces the rain that falls on the plot. Blocking the second displaces that,
plus whatever the upstream area delivers during the same storm, which is the
larger quantity by orders of magnitude.
chunks.source: MERIT Hydro v1.0.1, upstream drainage area band
chunks.title: Upstream drainage area is how much land drains through a point

chunks.body:
What can be tested is whether the reference this pipeline leans on is
reproducible by a different method over the same pixels in the same years. A
water index computed from Landsat 5 is scored against the JRC per-year
classification for 2003 to 2007, on a 6 by 4 grid with 8 blocks held out.

Blocks are contiguous tiles, not random pixels. Neighbouring pixels of one lake
are not independent samples and a pixel-wise split would inflate every score.
The threshold is fitted on training blocks only, and per-block scores are
reported alongside the pooled one.
chunks.source: validate.py, blockwise Landsat 5 MNDWI against the JRC yearly reference
chunks.title: The reference is checked against an independent spectral method

chunks.body:
Water then and water now are read from the same band of the same dataset: the
JRC transition classification, which compares the 1984 to 1999 record against
the 2000 to 2021 record across the whole Landsat archive using one method, at
30 m.

Using one source for both epochs is the point. A change detected inside a single
consistent classification is a change on the ground. A change detected between
two different classifications is partly a change of method, and there is no way
afterwards to say how much of it was which.
chunks.source: JRC Global Surface Water v1.4, transition and occurrence bands, Landsat archive 1984 to 2021
chunks.title: Both eras of water come from one source and one method

chunks.body:
The obvious approach is to classify water in an old composite, classify it in a
new one, and subtract. It cannot be made symmetric. The finer sensor finds more
water whatever is on the ground — narrow channels, pond margins, wet field
edges — so the subtraction reports water appearing wherever the newer sensor
simply looks harder.

Since the whole claim of this tool is water disappearing, a method with a known
bias toward finding water in the later epoch would undercut the one direction
that matters. The newer imagery is therefore shown, and used for land cover, but
never differenced for the water finding itself.
chunks.source: README, Method and where it is weak, on differencing Landsat against Sentinel-2
chunks.title: Why a Landsat composite is not differenced against a Sentinel-2 one

chunks.body:
Where the constraint is a drainage line rather than a bed, development can be
required to leave the channel physically open and build around it. The corridor
stays continuous, the plot keeps most of its area, and the obstruction this
screening flagged does not occur.

Singapore and Rotterdam both require this of sites on a watercourse. It is
harder architecturally than building over the line. The alignment that governs
is the notified one, not the terrain line this tool traced.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending the Singapore ABC Waters and Rotterdam water-square design standards
chunks.title: Build around the channel rather than over it

chunks.body:
Any site can discharge part of the requirement by recharging rather than
detaining: capturing what falls on the sealed surface and returning it to the
aquifer instead of to the drain. In a city that floods in the monsoon and runs
dry for the rest of the year, one structure answers both problems, which is why
this option needs no particular ground to be available.

How much it can absorb depends on what lies underneath, so it is sized on a
percolation test and not on this screening.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending the CGWB artificial recharge manual
chunks.title: Return the water to the aquifer instead of to the drain

chunks.body:
Where full restoration is not available, the site can be built as a designed
retention basin: a sunken park, dry for most of the year, which fills in heavy
rain and releases slowly afterwards. It reads as an amenity and behaves as a
tank, which is why it survives politically where a bare refusal does not.

Chennai and Ahmedabad have both built them. The volume such a basin must hold is
the displacement this screening already computed, so the sizing question is
answered before the design starts.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending the Chennai and Ahmedabad retention park programmes
chunks.title: A sunken park that holds the storm and looks like an amenity

chunks.body:
Where a plot sits on a mapped former bed, the use that discharges the retention
requirement completely is putting the water back. Restoration with public access
on the surrounding land gives the city an asset, and the development value moves
rather than disappearing, through transferable development rights or floor-space
credit exercised on another site.

Karnataka and Maharashtra both carry that mechanism. What is missing is
systematic use of it, which is a question of practice rather than of drafting.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending the Karnataka transferable development rights rules
chunks.title: Restoration with the development value moved elsewhere

chunks.body:
A conditions result means no buffer finding was made, but the plot stands very
low relative to the channel it drains into. Ground like that receives water
first and releases it last, whatever is built on it.

The conditions that follow are ordinary ones: on-site retention sized to hold
the runoff the development adds, and a plinth level set above the surrounding
ground. Neither is exotic and both are routinely imposed. The finding is that
they should be imposed here rather than left to the applicant's discretion, and
the height above drainage is the evidence for saying so.
chunks.source: index.html, the low-ground branch of decide()
chunks.title: What a conditions result means here

chunks.body:
A clear result means the tool found no recorded water body, no buffer breach and
no drainage line within the measurement uncertainty of the plot.

It is the weakest of the four statements, not the strongest. The other three are
positive findings backed by a measurement; this one is the absence of a finding,
and the record it draws on has a detection floor beneath which it is silent
rather than negative. Read as an instruction, it says this plot does not warrant
prioritising for investigation on satellite evidence. It does not say the plot
may be built on. Only the sanctioning authority says that.
chunks.source: index.html, the no-objection branch of decide()
chunks.title: What a clear result means here

chunks.body:
A referral does not decide the application either way. It identifies a specific
factual question that a survey can settle and that a satellite cannot, and it
asks for that survey.

For an applicant this is a delay with a defined end: establish the plot boundary
against the notified boundary, and the question is answered. For the authority
it is a filter that separates the applications needing a site visit from those
that do not. Treating every referral as an effective refusal, or waving them all
through, both discard the only information the outcome carries.
chunks.source: index.html, the OUTCOME table
chunks.title: A referral is not a refusal, and not a clearance

chunks.body:
A referral means the measurement cannot answer the question at the resolution
available, and names which question. Either a distance falls within the
uncertainty of its threshold, or the two shoreline records disagree, or a
terrain drainage line passes close enough that the notified alignment has to be
checked.

It is the outcome the tool reaches most often near a lake edge under the
narrower buffer regime, and that frequency is honest rather than evasive. The
action it asks for is specific and cheap: put a surveyor on the plot boundary
against the notified boundary, and the question resolves.
chunks.source: index.html, the referring branches of decide()
chunks.title: What a referral means here

chunks.body:
A rejection at screening means one of three things was found: the footprint
falls inside a water body still present in the record, it falls on a former
water body that held water in most observations, or it falls confidently inside
the configured buffer with the breach larger than the measurement uncertainty.

It is a recommendation to refuse at screening stage, addressed to the
sanctioning authority. It is not itself a refusal, and it does not by itself
establish that a structure already standing there is unlawful. What it does
establish is that the application should not proceed without the notified
boundary being checked on the ground.
chunks.source: index.html, the rejecting branches of decide()
chunks.title: What a rejection means here

chunks.body:
Measured from the water edge in the recent record this plot clears the buffer.
Measured from the edge in the earliest record it does not. The water body has
retreated here, and the distance between the two edges is reported.

This is the finding the tool exists to make. A setback drawn from today's
shoreline inherits whatever encroachment moved that shoreline, so a plot can
satisfy the buffer as measured and still sit inside the buffer as it would have
been drawn from the original boundary. Which boundary governs is a question for
the notified record, and the referral asks for exactly that.
chunks.source: index.html, the shoreline-disagreement branch of decide()
chunks.title: The two shoreline records disagree at this plot

chunks.body:
The survey added 1134 newly recorded drain encroachments to a standing list of
1963 still awaiting removal.

A queue of that length is not cleared in the order complaints arrive, and the
order it is cleared in decides who stays flooded. Ranking structures by how much
upstream catchment each one blocks is a way of ordering that queue by downstream
harm. The ranking is a proposal about priority, not a finding about legality.
chunks.source: BBMP stormwater drain encroachment survey, reported 2024
chunks.title: The removal queue is the thing this ranking is meant to order

chunks.body:
The same BBMP survey recorded 204 drain encroachments in Bommanahalli, placing
it fourth among the city's zones.

HSR Layout sits in that zone, and it is the densest cluster of satellite-derived
encroachment this tool finds anywhere in the study area. As with the other
zone-level figures this is corroboration at the scale of a zone. It says nothing
about any individual plot, and must never be repeated as though it did.
chunks.source: BBMP stormwater drain encroachment survey, reported 2024
chunks.title: Bommanahalli is fourth in the city

chunks.body:
BBMP identified 472 acres of encroached lake land and has recovered 17.38 acres
of it.

The gap between those two figures is the argument for screening before sanction
rather than enforcement afterwards. Land that is built on is, in practice, land
that stays built on. A plot checked at approval stage costs an officer a few
minutes; the same plot checked after construction costs years and usually ends
in the structure standing.
chunks.source: BBMP statement on the extent of encroached lake land
chunks.title: Detection is not the bottleneck; recovery is

chunks.body:
A BBMP survey recorded 523 stormwater drain encroachments in Mahadevapura, more
than in any other zone of the city.

Kasavanahalli, Panathur and Varthur all fall inside that zone, and they are
three of the four places this tool independently ranks highest. The tool has
never seen the survey: it reads satellites and terrain only. That the two line
up was not engineered, which is the only reason the agreement counts for
anything. It describes the zone, not any particular plot inside it.
chunks.source: BBMP stormwater drain encroachment survey, reported 2024
chunks.title: Mahadevapura leads the city for recorded drain encroachments

chunks.body:
The two largest water bodies in this catchment survive as water on the satellite
record while being, in fact, heavily degraded: froth carried onto adjacent
roads, surface fires, and inflow dominated by untreated sewage.

This matters for reading the map honestly. A lake shown as present is a lake
that still holds water in the record. Nothing in this tool measures water
quality, ecological function or whether the water body performs the storage role
its protection assumes. Present is not the same as intact.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending a citable record of the Bellandur and Varthur froth and fire incidents
chunks.title: The surviving lakes here are not in good condition

chunks.body:
Bengaluru Urban and Rural hold 1547 lakes between them, with 10785 acres of lake
land recorded as encroached.

This study area covers two zones of one city. The figures above are the reason
the method matters more than this particular catchment: a screening check that
runs from public satellite data can be pointed at any of those lakes without new
fieldwork, and the constraint on doing so is attention rather than data.
chunks.source: BBMP statement on lake counts and encroached extent across Bengaluru Urban and Rural
chunks.title: The scale across the district

chunks.body:
The flooding that closed the Outer Ring Road and inundated tech parks and
apartment complexes concentrated in the same zones this tool ranks highest for
lost water and blocked flow paths.

That correspondence is evidence that the mechanism is real at catchment scale.
It is not evidence about any particular plot, it is not a prediction that the
same places flood next time, and it must never be offered as one. Citation still
required before this is used in anything that leaves the building.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending a citable record of the 2022 Bengaluru flooding in Mahadevapura and along the Outer Ring Road
chunks.title: The zones that flooded are the zones that filled their tanks

chunks.body:
Structures built inside lake and drain buffers in this city have been the
subject of removal orders. The risk a buffer finding represents to an applicant
is therefore not only that sanction is refused, but that a building completed
under a defective sanction is later ordered down.

That is the practical case for screening at approval stage. It is also a general
statement about a line of orders, not advice about any specific plot, and the
specific orders must be cited before this is relied on.
chunks.source: PLACEHOLDER pending the specific NGT and High Court orders directing removal of buffer-zone structures in Bengaluru
chunks.title: Structures inside the buffer have been ordered removed

chunks.body:
The building layer is machine-derived footprint geometry. It carries no name, no
khata, no survey number and no owner, and nothing in this tool links a footprint
to a person.

A flagged footprint is a location to check against records held elsewhere. Any
attribution of responsibility for it comes from those records and from a site
visit, not from here. Naming or implying a party on the strength of a satellite
flag would be unsupported by the evidence and unfair to whoever was named.
chunks.source: The scope of the datasets this tool reads
chunks.title: No person, owner or occupant can be identified from this

chunks.body:
Costing flood damage needs asset values, occupancy, depth-damage relationships
and a frequency of occurrence. This tool has none of them and cannot produce a
monetary figure for the harm a development causes or the loss a flood inflicts.

Where a cost is what is actually wanted, the volume and the exposure class are
the inputs to hand to someone who holds the rest. Producing a rupee figure from
what is here would require inventing the missing terms, and the number would
carry the authority of the measured ones without their basis.
chunks.source: The scope of the datasets this tool reads
chunks.title: No damage, cost or compensation figure can be produced

chunks.body:
Asked whether an application will be approved, this tool has nothing to say. It
does not know the sanction record, the applicant, the local practice or which
buffer regime the deciding officer applies.

What it can say is what a screening check against a stated ruleset finds, and
what the deciding authority would have to resolve before deciding. Converting
that into a likelihood of approval would mean modelling the authority rather
than the ground, which is a different exercise and not one this evidence
supports.
chunks.source: index.html, the comment above decide()
chunks.title: Whether the authority will approve is not predicted here

chunks.body:
Producing a defensible flood depth for a plot needs four things this tool does
not have: the geometry and condition of the drain network carrying water away, a
fine-resolution elevation model rather than a coarse global one, a local
intensity-duration-frequency curve, and a hydraulic solver routing water over
that surface with stated boundary conditions.

Without them a depth would be a guess wearing a unit. Naming the four missing
inputs is more useful than producing one, because it tells whoever needs the
answer what to go and commission.
chunks.source: index.html, the stated scope of the terrain layers
chunks.title: What a real flood-depth answer would require

chunks.body:
This is an evidence tool, not a flood predictor. It reports what the satellite
record shows was water, what the terrain says about where water runs, and how
much additional runoff a development generates.

It does not say whether a place will flood, when, how often, or how deep. Those
are outputs of a hydraulic model with inputs this tool does not hold. Asked a
flooding question, the answerable part is the displaced volume and the
topographic exposure, and the unanswerable part should be named rather than
approximated.
chunks.source: README, the opening statement of scope
chunks.title: This tool does not predict flooding

chunks.body:
Whether a particular construction is lawful depends on the notified boundary,
the sanction record, the date of the sanction, the title and the buffer regime
that binds that application. This tool holds none of those, and reads only
satellite and terrain data.

It reports measurements and compares them against a buffer figure it has been
told to apply. That is a screening input for the authority that decides, and for
the applicant it is a reason to check something specific. It is not an opinion
on legality and cannot be cited as one.
chunks.source: index.html, the certificate footer and the ruleset comment
chunks.title: This is not legal advice or a legal determination

chunks.body:
Every distance here is measured between raster features, not between marked
corners. The plot is an assumed square centred on a click, not a surveyed
boundary, and the water edge is a classification boundary, not a notified one.

A screening result narrows what a surveyor needs to check and tells them where
to start. It does not stand in for the visit. The certificate carries an
unsigned ground-verification block for that reason, and a certificate without
that block completed is a lead rather than a record.
chunks.source: index.html, the ground-verification sign-off block on the certificate
chunks.title: This does not replace a survey

chunks.body:
The layers cover one rectangle. A point outside it has no measurement, and the
tool returns a referral saying so rather than a value.

Nothing is reported for such a point: no distance, no exposure class and no
displaced volume. A volume computed for a plot the tool holds no evidence about
would be arithmetic on assumptions alone, which is indistinguishable in
appearance from a measurement and is not one. Extending coverage is a matter of
re-running the extraction over a different rectangle.
chunks.source: index.html, the first branch of decide()
chunks.title: Outside the mapped rectangle there is no evidence at all

chunks.body:
An applicant measures their setback from the water's edge as it stands today.
Where the lake has already shrunk, that edge is itself the product of earlier
encroachment, and a buffer drawn from it lands somewhere a buffer drawn from the
original boundary would not.

This tool measures both: from the water edge in the recent record and from the
edge in the earliest record available. When the two disagree by more than one
source pixel it says so and refers the plot, because the question of which
boundary governs is a legal one about the notified boundary, not a question the
satellite record can settle.
chunks.source: index.html, the shoreline-disagreement branch of decide()
chunks.title: A buffer measured from today's shoreline can be a buffer from an encroachment

chunks.body:
Karnataka has more than one buffer figure in play. This tool does not decide
which one binds a given application. It applies the ruleset it is told to apply
and records that choice, with its citation, on the screening certificate.

Changing the ruleset changes the outcome, and it is meant to. An officer
selecting the narrower regime and an officer selecting the wider one will get
different screening results from identical measurements, and both results are
correct reports of what was asked.

The measurements themselves do not change with the ruleset. Only the threshold
they are compared against does.
chunks.source: index.html, RULESETS
chunks.title: Buffer distances are operator configuration, not a determination by this tool

chunks.body:
A buffer is breached if any part of the plot falls inside it, so every distance
here is the nearest approach over the assumed footprint, not the distance from
its centre. Taking the centre, or the maximum, would pass every corner plot that
clips a lake edge.

The footprint is an assumption, not a measurement. The tool assumes a square
plot of the stated frontage centred on the click, and the frontage is operator
input. Enlarging it moves every distance closer and can change the outcome,
which is why the assumed frontage is printed on the certificate beside the
distances it produced.
chunks.source: index.html, the minimum reduction in readSite()
chunks.title: A buffer applies to the footprint, so the nearest corner governs

chunks.body:
The wider buffer was applied prospectively, to sanctions granted after the
order, rather than as an instruction to demolish everything already standing
inside it. A structure predating the order is not automatically unlawful by
virtue of its distance from a lake.

That distinction matters for what this tool's output can be used for. A plot
screened before construction is squarely within scope. An existing structure
flagged by the same measurement is a lead for the authority that holds the
sanction record, not a finding that the building is illegal.
chunks.source: NGT O.A. 222/2014 and the Supreme Court order on its application
chunks.title: The wider buffer was applied prospectively

chunks.body:
The mapped area is the Bellandur and Varthur catchment, falling in the
Bommanahalli and Mahadevapura zones of BBMP. Plan sanction, drain alignment
records and encroachment removal for a plot here sit with that authority.

Outside the mapped rectangle this tool holds no evidence at all. It does not
degrade gracefully beyond the boundary; it stops. A click outside returns a
referral saying so, and no measurement, distance or volume is reported for it,
because a number computed from absent evidence would be a fabrication.
chunks.source: index.html, the CITIES table
chunks.title: Study area and which authority holds it

chunks.body:
The National Green Tribunal fixed a 75 m no-construction buffer around lakes and
50 m around primary stormwater drains, measured from the boundary outward. The
Supreme Court upheld it.

This is the wider of the two regimes. It is also the one this tool can test
confidently: 75 m is comfortably outside the measurement uncertainty, so a plot
inside it can be called inside it rather than referred.

The buffer is a prohibition on construction, not a taking of title. A plot may
be lawfully owned and still be unbuildable.
chunks.source: NGT O.A. 222/2014, Forward Foundation v. State of Karnataka, upheld by the Supreme Court
chunks.title: NGT 75 m lake buffer, upheld by the Supreme Court

chunks.body:
Under the state revision applied at plan sanction, no construction is permitted
within 30 m of a lake boundary or 25 m of a stormwater drain, measured from the
notified boundary outward.

This is the narrower of the two regimes in play in Karnataka. An officer knows
which one binds them; the tool applies the one it is told to and records that
choice on the certificate.

Read together with the error budget: at the stated measurement uncertainty this
buffer sits barely outside the error bar, so most near-lake plots screen as
refer-to-survey rather than reject. That is a property of the rule, not a defect
in the measurement.
chunks.source: State revision of the NGT buffer, as applied by BBMP in plan sanction
chunks.title: State revision — 30 m lake buffer, 25 m drain buffer

chunks.body:
The lake boundary in this tool is the edge of a satellite water classification.
The boundary that binds an application is the one in the notified record held by
the revenue department and the lake authority.

Where they agree, the screening result is a fair preview of the survey result.
Where they disagree, the notified boundary wins and the screening result was a
lead that did its job by prompting the check.

Nothing here substitutes for a physical survey of the plot against that
boundary. The certificate carries a sign-off block for exactly that reason.
chunks.source: index.html, the ground-verification block of the screening certificate
chunks.title: The notified lake boundary governs, not the satellite edge

chunks.body:
There are 4 outcomes and deliberately none of them is approve. This screens; it
does not grant permission.

The best available outcome is that nothing was found — no recorded water body,
no buffer breach, no drainage line within the measurement uncertainty of the
plot. That is a statement about the satellite record, not a licence.

Asked whether a construction should be allowed, the honest answer is what the
record shows and what it cannot show, followed by who decides. The deciding
authority is the sanctioning authority. It is never this tool, and it is never
the model reading this.
chunks.source: index.html, the OUTCOME table and the comment above decide()
chunks.title: None of the outcomes is an approval

chunks.body:
What this tool calls a drainage line is a channel derived from a terrain model.
It is where water runs downhill. A rajakaluve is a drain with a notified
alignment, a width and a survey record, and the two are related but not the
same object.

Where the terrain says water flows and the record shows no drain, that is worth
checking and nothing more. Where the record shows a drain, the record governs.
The tool therefore never rejects a plot on drainage evidence alone; it refers it
to the alignment held against that survey number.
chunks.source: BBMP stormwater drain survey and the notified rajakaluve alignment
chunks.title: The BBMP rajakaluve alignment governs, not the terrain model

chunks.body:
Protection of a tank attaches to the tank as recorded land, not to whether it
currently holds water. A tank bed that has dried, silted or been levelled
remains tank land in the record until the record says otherwise.

This is why the historic water edge is measured at all. A plot that is
comfortably clear of every present-day shoreline may still sit on recorded tank
bed, and the satellite record from the earlier epoch is often the only readily
available evidence that it does. The record to check against is the revenue
entry for that survey number.
chunks.source: Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority Act and the lake-protection line of orders
chunks.title: Tanks are protected as a class, not only when they hold water

chunks.body:
The building footprint layer for this city has not been exported, so no ranked
structures, per-building evidence or neighbourhood context is available. Every
other layer works without it.

That means an answer here can describe the ground under the plot and cannot say
what is already standing on or near it, and it should say so rather than leaving
the omission to be inferred. Producing the layer is one export task in the
extraction step; until it runs, statements about nearby flagged structures are
unavailable rather than negative.
chunks.source: index.html, the optional building layer in loadCity()
chunks.title: The ranked building layer is not loaded

chunks.body:
The water classification compares 1984 to 1999 against 2000 to 2021. The
imagery on screen is an early composite scrubbed against a recent one, and
neither is the source of the water layers. The land cover used to confirm
construction is from the most recent years only. The last-water-year channel
spans the whole classification archive.

These are four different windows and conflating them produces confident
nonsense. A lake visible on the older imagery is not the same statement as a
pixel in the historic classification. State which window a claim comes from.
chunks.source: index.html, the timeline readout and the layer definitions
chunks.title: Four different time frames are in play, and they are not interchangeable

chunks.body:
It reconstructs a city's lost water bodies from the satellite record, flags the
buildings standing on them, ranks those by how much catchment they block, and
screens any plot before it is built on.

Three modes: a timeline showing what was there and what happened to it, a plot
check giving a screening decision against a selectable buffer regime, and a
downstream view of the low ground receiving the runoff the lost tanks used to
hold. Everything it reports traces to a published dataset and a stated
threshold.
chunks.source: README, the opening
chunks.title: What this tool is
